text.title: Chaos-Eval Core Rules
text.summary: Four testable rules every chaos-eval run enforces.

rule.statement: Each tool has a documented fault catalogue: at minimum timeout, http_5xx, rate_limit, corrupted_return, disconnect. Each entry includes default injection rate.
rule.rationale: Untyped chaos is impossible to reproduce; catalogues make runs comparable across versions.

rule.statement: Faults are injected at deterministic seeds along the agent trajectory; the same seed reproduces the same fault sequence.
rule.rationale: Random injection without seed makes regressions look like noise.

rule.statement: The rubric grades each fault occurrence on a 0..3 scale: 0=confidently wrong, 1=fails silently, 2=escalates / stops cleanly, 3=retries intelligently and succeeds.
rule.rationale: Binary success/fail hides the distinction between "stopped cleanly" and "confidently wrong"; the latter is the dangerous case.

rule.statement: A clean (no-fault) baseline is run first on the same eval set; chaos-eval scores are reported alongside baseline, not in isolation.
rule.rationale: Without baseline a 70% chaos score is meaningless — could be a flaky model or hard set.

rule.statement: When the replay harness, the per-tool fault catalogue and the recovery rubric are all present, the chaos-eval runs baseline and fault-injected passes on the same eval set and seed, and the report carries a 0..3 score per fault class plus `confidently_wrong_count`; promotion is blocked while that count is above 0. When any tool in the inventory lacks one of the five fault classes (timeout, http_5xx, rate_limit, corrupted_return, disconnect) or its injection rate, the run MUST NOT start — the catalogue is completed first, rates taken from the last 30 days of production stats, not guessed.

rationale.source: Rosenthal and Jones, Chaos Engineering (O'Reilly 2020); 04-procedure step 5 decision gate

rule.rationale: Chaos Engineering (Rosenthal and Jones, O'Reilly 2020) makes the same demand of any fault experiment: a steady-state baseline and a written hypothesis before injection, or the result cannot be attributed. A partial catalogue produces a score for the tools that were catalogued and silence for the one that fails in production, which is exactly the confidently-wrong case the method exists to catch.

rule.statement: When no replay harness with a deterministic seed and stubbed tools exists, faults MUST NOT be injected into live tools or hand-written one-off mocks, and no chaos score is reported for the agent. The harness is built first per agent-replay-harness-cookbook, and the chaos-eval report names it in `harness_ref`; a report without that field is rejected by the validator.
rule.rationale: Injecting a 503 into a real dependency tests the dependency's on-call, not the agent, and an ad-hoc mock gives a fault sequence nobody can replay when the score drops next release. The Principles of Chaos Engineering require experiments to be controlled and repeatable; without the harness neither holds, so the run is noise with a number attached.

rule.statement: When the harness and catalogue exist but no recovery rubric does, chaos trajectories MUST NOT be graded pass/fail as a stopgap. The rubric is authored first: the four outcome classes (0 confidently wrong, 1 silent failure, 2 clean stop or escalation, 3 intelligent retry that succeeds), one worked trajectory from the eval set per class, and sign-off by the named QA owner before the first fault-injected run.

rationale.source: Zheng et al. 2023, Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena; 03-rubric practice of this methodology

rule.rationale: Pass/fail on a fault run scores "stopped cleanly and told the user" the same as "invented an answer", which erases the one distinction the method is for. Zheng et al. (2023), "Judging LLM-as-a-Judge", show grader agreement depends on an explicit rubric with anchored examples; an LLM judge asked to grade recovery without one drifts toward rewarding fluent wrong answers.
